query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A pre-oxidation treatment that promotes the formation of a continuous, Cr-rich (Cr2O3) oxide layer on FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings improves high‐temperature wear resistance by acting as a protective barrier that mitigates adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.material_initial_state: Untreated FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., controlled air exposure or mild thermal oxidation) prior to high-temperature wear testing to foster the development of a Cr-rich oxide layer.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear testing at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900 °C) under high normal loads and high sliding speeds representative of high-temperature service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous Cr-rich oxide (i.e., Cr2O3) layer formed on the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The Cr-rich oxide layer acts as a stable, lubricious barrier under high temperature that reduces direct metallic contact, limits adhesive bonding and plastic deformation at asperities, and thereby lowers overall material loss during wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-oxidized coatings should display a continuous Cr2O3 layer on the surface, exhibit lower friction coefficients, reduced adhesive/oxidative wear (lower specific wear rate), and less debris formation compared to an untreated (baseline) coating under the same high-temperature and high-load conditions.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating without pre-oxidation treatment, which would typically develop a less continuous or less protective oxide layer under high-temperature wear conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold within the temperature range of about 700–900 °C and under high normal loads where friction-induced heating and oxidation are significant; outside of these conditions, different wear mechanisms or oxide behaviors may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise efficacy of the pre-oxidation treatment in consistently forming a uniform Cr-rich oxide layer on complex multicomponent alloys is uncertain, as local compositional variations and processing history may influence oxide continuity and mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings on conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to the pre-oxidation treatment (as described) and leave the other untreated. Then perform high-temperature wear testing at 700–900 °C under the same high normal load and sliding conditions. Characterize the worn surfaces using SEM/EDS to assess oxide layer continuity and analyze wear rates, friction coefficients, and wear debris generation.
measurements: Surface oxide composition and thickness (via SEM/EDS and possibly XPS).
Friction coefficient profiles during wear testing.
Wear track morphology to identify signs of adhesive, oxidative, and plastic deformation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not display a continuous Cr-rich oxide layer or if they exhibit similar or higher wear rates, friction coefficients, and damage modes compared to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis that the Cr-rich oxide layer governs improved high-temperature wear resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It is also a well-known fact that materials generally have thin films or layers of oxide on their surface. This oxide layer initially hinders the sliding parts from coming into direct contact which will be broken with ease when the load applied is increased. This removal of the oxide layer on the surface results in direct contact between the sliding parts. Higher contact pressure at the higher load results in fracture of the oxide layer that exposes the pin material to the hard counter disc which in turn induces plastic deformation. The exposed pin material welds together with the hard counter disc surface due to higher contact pressure and the welded material delaminates from the soft surface due to sliding action. The welded mixed material usually comes out as wear debris and sometimes it is transferred to hard material from the soft material surface as a film. This loss of material in the form of wear debris or transferred layer at the higher loading conditions results in increased wear loss. Hence, the rate of wear for the base copper and surface composites with HEA reinforcement increases at higher loads.
